This Judgment shall decide the instant appeal preferred by the appellants under Section 70 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 as amended upto date (hereinafter referred as 'FSS Act')
assailing impugned order dated 27.10.2021 passed by the Ld. Adjudicating Officer/Addl. District Magistrate (East), in case title as 'FSO v. Shrey Kumar & Ors.' under Section 52 of FSS Act, imposing penalty of Rs. 7 Lakhs in total upon the five appellants.

FACTUAL BACKGROUND:
2. Briefly stated, it is the case of the appellants that Sh. Shrey Kumar S/o Sh. Krishan Kumar is the Authorised representative appellant No. 3 company viz., M/s Aadvik Foods and Products Pvt. Ltd.
whereas Sh. Hitesh Rathi is the nominee and Sh. Rakesh H. Thakkar is the nominee of appellant no.5 M/s Ruchi Foods LLP, having its registered office at Ground Floor, Piyush Cottage, Parabia Compound, Opp Express Hotel Alkapuri, Vadodara, Gujarat - 390007, which incidentally is the manufacturer of the food item. It is stated that Sh. Naresh Kumar Sharma, Food Safety Officer (in short "FSO") on 06.07.2020 took a sample of "Camel Milk Powder" for analysis from the Food Business OperatorcumDirector Sh. Shrey Kumar S/o Sh. Krishan Kumar (in short "FBO") from the premises of appellant no.3 company M/s Aadvik Foods and Products Pvt. Ltd. situated at 2 nd Floor, Plot No. 475, Patparganj Industrial Area, New Delhi110092, where the said food article was stored for sale for human consumption; and that the sample consisted of 8 packets each 150 kg sealed packets in original condition with identical batch number and label declaration, each stated to be containing "Camel Milk Powder"; and that each packet was separately marked, packed,
fastened and sealed by the FSO, for which a payment of Rs.5,200/ was paid in terms of notice in the prescribed Form VA towards cost of the 08 nos. of packets; and notice in Form VA in terms of 2.4.1(4) of FSS Rules, 2011 was prepared and sent to appellant no.5.

The impugned order is assailed in the present appeal by the appellants primarily on the grounds that there was no violation of Regulation 2.2.2.10 of FSS (P&L) Regulation, 2011 since "the best before statement"

Industries v State of Bihar & Anr., 2011 FAC 265; and that there was no violation of Regulation 2.2.2 (f)(i) of FSS (P&L) Regulation 2011, since the standards of Flavoured Milk Powder in dried form have been specifically given on the label of the food item and the requirement of quantitative disclosure of ingredients by giving percentage of cocoa powder was not required and that the declaration of percentage of ingredients was only required if the food item was non standardized and being sold as mixture or combination of various ingredients, which was not an issue in the present matter; and that the ld AO/ADM failed to appreciate that the ingredients mixed or contained did loose their identity and could not be separated out and no fixed composition has been prescribed by law, as is the case with products such as Corn Flax Mixture, Muesli Dry Fruit.

sentences.text:
At the outset, the impugned order dated 27.10.2021 passed by the Ld.
Adjudicating Officer/ADM cannot be sustained in law.
First thing first, the decision that the food item was a "proprietary item" cannot be sustained in law .

The term 'proprietary item' is defined by Regulation 2.12 of the FSS (FPS&FA) Regulation),
which reads as under:
"2.12 PROPRIETARY FOOD [2.12.1: For the purpose of these regulations, (1)
Proprietary food means an article of food that has not been standardised under these regulations, but does not include novel foods, foods for special dietary uses, foods for special medical purposes, functional foods, nutraceuticals, health supplements and such other food articles which the Central Government may notify in this behalf:

Provided that any deviation in quality parameters of a standardised food, as specified in the Food Safety and Standards Regulations made under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 shall not qualify the resultant product as a proprietary food.

(2)
Proprietary food shall contain only those ingredients other than additives which are either standardised or permitted for use in the preparation of other standardised food under these Regulations, except the ingredients which may be specified by the Authority from time to time.
Provided that a proprietary food may also contain vitamins and minerals in quantities not exceeding one RDA of the respective micronutrients.
(3) Proprietary food shall use only such additives and at such levels, as specified for the Category or Subcategory under Appendix A of these Regulations, to which the food belongs.
Such category or Subcategory shall be clearly mentioned on the label along with the generic name, nature and composition of the proprietary food.
(4) Proprietary food shall comply with the microbiological requirements as specified in Appendix B of these Regulations.

If no microbiological standards are specified for any foods or food categories in Appendix B of these regulations, proprietary foods failing under such food categories shall not contain any pathogenic microorganism at a level that may render the food product unsafe.

(5)
Proprietary food shall also comply with the provisions, as applicable, of all other regulations made under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
No health claims shall be made in respect of proprietary by adequate and scientific evidence.

(6) The Food Business Operator shall be fully Sh. Shrey Kumar S/O Sh. Krishan Kumar vs Food Safety Officer on 20 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/13925913/
5 responsible for safety of the proprietary food in respect of human consumption.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 12. A bare perusal of the aforesaid Regulation would show that proprietary food item would be such article of food for which there are no standardised regulations.

Ld. Counsel for the appellants was very right in pointing out that the food item in question was under the category of "flavoured milk",
which is defined by Regulation 2.1.3 of the FSS (FPS&FA) Regulation), as under: "2.1.2 Standard of flavoured milk.
This standard applies to Flavoured Milk as defined in item 1 of this subregulation.
1. Description.

"Flavoured Milk" means the product prepared from milk or other products derived from milk, or both, and edible flavourings with or without addition of sugar, nutritive, sweeteners,
other nondairy ingredients including, stabilisers and food colours.

Flavoured milk shall be subjected to heat treatment as provided in subregulation 2.2.1 (General Standards for Milk and Milk Products) Where flavoured milk is dried or concentrated, the dried or concentrated product on addition of prescribed amount of water shall give a product conforming to the requirements of flavoured milk.

entities.text: General Standards for Milk and Milk Products)
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: 2. Essential Composition and Quality Factors.
(a) Raw Material.
(i) Milk (ii) Concentrated and dried milk (iii) Milk fat, cream, butter and butter oil (iv) Potable water for use in reconstitution or recombination (b) Permitted ingredients.
Flavoured milk shall have the same minimum percentage of milk fat and milk solidsnotfat as that of the milk, as provided for in the Standard for Milk, from which it is prepared.
3. Food Additives.

For products covered under this standard, specific food additives specified in Appendix 'A' of these regulations may be used and only within the limits specified."

6 13.

On a careful perusal of proceedings done at the spot recorded vide Form VA and the lable on the food item, which is Annexure 1 to this Judgment, it is clearly brought out that that food additives which were added in the product had already been printed as soya lecithin (E 322) and Xanthum gum (E 415) in the prescribed notice in form VA.
It appears that food item in question was wrongly treated as proprietary food and analyzed such on the wrong presumption that sample had no standardised parametres under the aforesaid Regulations.

14. Secondly, the decision as regards violation of Regulation 2.2.2.10 of the FSS (P&L) Regulation about 'nondeclaration of best before/expiry not being in capital letters' was a trivial infringement of the Regulation that was also not actionable in view of decision in the case Pramod Kumar Kedia v.
State of Bihar (supra); Oscar Joseph & Anr v State of Jharkhand & Ors and M.D. Anand Aqua M/s S.N.B. Industries v State of Bihar & Anr (supra), wherein it was categorically held that even writing 'best before statement' in small letters was sufficient compliance for regulation 2.2.2 (10) of the FSS (Labelling and Packaging) Regulations, 2011.

15. Be that as it may, it was brought out that the mandate to providing the 'best before date/expiry'
date in capital letters has since been abolished as per Gazette Notification No. 1 94/FSSA/SP/Labelling/2014(p II dated 17.01.2020, which became effective from 01.01.2022,
and therefore, benefit of such dilution of mandate has to be given retrospectively to the appellant Nos. 4 to 5, for which reference can be invited to decision in the cas case of B.L. Kohli v. Delhi Administration, by the Hon'ble Judge of the High Court of Delhi, New Delhi cited as 1986(3) FSS 140.

entities.text: High Court of Delhi, New Delhi
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
It also goes without saying that as per recommendation of the FSSAI conveyed vide letter dated 17.01.2020 as explained in Anneuxre1 with the said letter, defect of noncompliance about the "capital letters" mentioned on the label of the food product was held to be a minor and curable defect and it was advised that prosecution may not be launched in the said case.
16. Thirdly, in so far as violation of Regulation 2.2.2.2(f)(i) of the FSS (Labelling and Packaging)
Regulations, 2011 is concerned, it reads as under:

"(f) Every package of food sold as a mixture or combination shall disclose the percentage of the ingredient used at the time of the manufacture of the food (including compound ingredients or categories of ingredients), if such ingredient (i) is emphasised as present on the label through words or pictures or graphics; or (ii) is not within the name of the food but, is essential to characterize the food and is expected to be present in the food by consumers, and if the omission of the quantitative ingredient declaration will mislead or deceive the consumer:
Provided that where the ingredient has been used as flavouring agent, the disclosure of such ingredient is not required:
Provided further that where the drained net weight is indicated on the label as required or in case of such food products where specific provisions are stipulated under these Regulations or where a pictorial representation of a serving suggestion is made for consumer information and use, the disclosure of such ingredient is not Sh. 7 required.

sentences.text: Provided further that in case of any bottle containing liquid milk or liquid beverage having milk as an ingredient, soft drink, carbonated water or readyto serve fruit beverages, the declarations with regard to addition of fruit pulp and fruit juice shall invariably appear on the body of the bottle."

17. A careful perusal of the aforesaid provision when analysed visa vis proceedings done vide notice form VA would bring out that there was no necessity of quantitative disclosure of the ingredients and/or for giving percentage of cocoa powder, which was required only if the food article is nonstandardised and is sold as mixture of combination.

A bare perusal of the label of food item would show that graphic was not with regard to Cocoa powder and what has been shown is the heap of product itself, which is a brown coloured powder form and nowhere the heap is shown on the label as cocoa powder.

At the cost of repetition, the food item was camel milk powder (dried form),
which was being sold as standardised product manufacture/prepared from various basic ingredients such as camel milk, sugar, cocoa powder and various other additives as mentioned on the notice VA and the ingredients used were not separable or retrievable out in any manner or by any chemical method and thus remaining in same physical form or means.
There are no grounds to suggest that the label was such that might have mislead or deceived the ultimate consumers of the food items.

18. Therefore, the offence of misbranding of the product within the meaning of Section 3(ii) (2f) of the FSS Act did not arise for consideration and in any case the prosecution against the appellants No.1 to 3 was saved by virtue of Section 80(B) (2)(d) of the FSS Act since it was being sold in same packed condition by the FBO as was purchased from the manufacturer viz. , Appellant no. 5, and thus defence of due diligence was available against the appellant Nos. 1 to 3 who were able to demonstrate that they had purchased the food item in ordinary course of business believing the same conforming all necessary parameters/standard.

All said and done, it is manifest that during the proceedings before the Adjudicating Officer/ADM the appellant Nos. 4 and 5 also rectified the defects on the label in good faith and the prosecution against them was totally unwarranted.

FINAL ORDER:
19.
In view of the foregoing discussion, I find that the impugned order dated 27.10.2021 passed by the Adjudicating Officer/ADM cannot be sustained in law, and therefore, same is hereby set aside.
The sentence awarded by the Adjudicating Officer/ADM for contravention of Section 52 read with Section 49 of the FSS Act imposing penalty against the appellants are hereby set aside.

The FD of Rs.
3.50 Lacs placed on the record in compliance of direction of this Court dated 26.11.2021 be returned to the appellants.
20. The Record of the Adjudicating Officer /ADM be returned along with the copy of the order.
File of appeal be consigned to the Record Room.

Shrey Kumar S/O Sh. Krishan Kumar vs Food Safety Officer on 20 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/13925913/
2 to file an appeal against the report of the Food Analyst.
It is also a matter of record that the food article i.e. "Camel Milk Powder" was manufactured, packed or further supplied by appellant no. 5 M/s Ruchi Foods LLP, to appellant no.3 company viz. M/s Aadvik Foods and Products Pvt. Ltd.,
vide invoice dated 04.06.2020 and appellant no.4 Sh. Rakesh H. Thakkar was the Incharge and responsible for the conduct and daytoday business of appellant no. 5 M/s Ruchi Foods LLP.
5.
The above said accused/ respondents violating the provision of Section 23 (1)
and Section 26(1) & 26 (2) (ii), Section 27(2)(c) read with Section 3(1)(zf) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and violated Regulation No. 2.2.2.2 (f)(i) and 2.2.2.10 of The Food Safety and Standards (Packaging & Labelling) Regulation, 2011 and also violated Regulation no. 2.12.1.3 of the Food Safety & Standards (Food Products Standards & Food Additives) Regulation, 2011 which is punishable U/s 52 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
It is contravention of provisions of FSS Act, 2006 by the above named respondents.
The impugned order is assailed in the present appeal by the appellants primarily on the grounds that there was no violation of Regulation 2.2.2.10 of FSS (P&L) Regulation, 2011 since "the best before statement"
was depicted in small letters, which was sufficient compliance for which reference is placed in decision in Parmod Kumar Kedia v State of Bihar, 2012(1) FAC 479, Oscar Joseph & Anr v State of Jharkhand & Ors., 2012(2) FAC 74 and M.D. Anand Aqua M/s S.N.B. Industries v State of Bihar & Anr., 2011 FAC 265; and that there was no violation of Regulation 2.2.2 (f)(i) of FSS (P&L) Regulation 2011, since the standards of Flavoured Milk Powder in dried form have been specifically given on the label of the food item and the requirement of quantitative disclosure of ingredients by giving percentage of cocoa powder was not required and that the declaration of percentage of ingredients was only required if the food item was non standardized and being sold as mixture or combination of various ingredients, which was not an issue in the present matter; and that the ld AO/ADM failed to appreciate that the ingredients mixed or contained did loose their identity and could not be separated out and no fixed composition has been prescribed by law, as is the case with products such as Corn Flax Mixture, Muesli Dry Fruit.
opennyai_summary.issue: First thing first, the decision that the food item was a "proprietary item" cannot be sustained in law .
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
12. A bare perusal of the aforesaid Regulation would show that proprietary food item would be such article of food for which there are no standardised regulations.
It appears that food item in question was wrongly treated as proprietary food and analyzed such on the wrong presumption that sample had no standardised parametres under the aforesaid Regulations.
14. Secondly, the decision as regards violation of Regulation 2.2.2.10 of the FSS (P&L) Regulation about 'nondeclaration of best before/expiry not being in capital letters' was a trivial infringement of the Regulation that was also not actionable in view of decision in the case Pramod Kumar Kedia v.
State of Bihar (supra); Oscar Joseph & Anr v State of Jharkhand & Ors and M.D. Anand Aqua M/s S.N.B. Industries v State of Bihar & Anr (supra), wherein it was categorically held that even writing 'best before statement' in small letters was sufficient compliance for regulation 2.2.2 (10) of the FSS (Labelling and Packaging) Regulations, 2011.
15. Be that as it may, it was brought out that the mandate to providing the 'best before date/expiry'
date in capital letters has since been abolished as per Gazette Notification No. 1 94/FSSA/SP/Labelling/2014(p II dated 17.01.2020, which became effective from 01.01.2022,
and therefore, benefit of such dilution of mandate has to be given retrospectively to the appellant Nos. 4 to 5, for which reference can be invited to decision in the cas case of B.L. Kohli v. Delhi Administration, by the Hon'ble Judge of the High Court of Delhi, New Delhi cited as 1986(3) FSS 140.
17. A careful perusal of the aforesaid provision when analysed visa vis proceedings done vide notice form VA would bring out that there was no necessity of quantitative disclosure of the ingredients and/or for giving percentage of cocoa powder, which was required only if the food article is nonstandardised and is sold as mixture of combination.
A bare perusal of the label of food item would show that graphic was not with regard to Cocoa powder and what has been shown is the heap of product itself, which is a brown coloured powder form and nowhere the heap is shown on the label as cocoa powder.
At the cost of repetition, the food item was camel milk powder (dried form),
which was being sold as standardised product manufacture/prepared from various basic ingredients such as camel milk, sugar, cocoa powder and various other additives as mentioned on the notice VA and the ingredients used were not separable or retrievable out in any manner or by any chemical method and thus remaining in same physical form or means.
There are no grounds to suggest that the label was such that might have mislead or deceived the ultimate consumers of the food items.
18. Therefore, the offence of misbranding of the product within the meaning of Section 3(ii) (2f) of the FSS Act did not arise for consideration and in any case the prosecution against the appellants No.1 to 3 was saved by virtue of Section 80(B) (2)(d) of the FSS Act since it was being sold in same packed condition by the FBO as was purchased from the manufacturer viz. , Appellant no. 5, and thus defence of due diligence was available against the appellant Nos. 1 to 3 who were able to demonstrate that they had purchased the food item in ordinary course of business believing the same conforming all necessary parameters/standard.
All said and done, it is manifest that during the proceedings before the Adjudicating Officer/ADM the appellant Nos. 4 and 5 also rectified the defects on the label in good faith and the prosecution against them was totally unwarranted.
opennyai_summary.decision:
FINAL ORDER:
19.
In view of the foregoing discussion, I find that the impugned order dated 27.10.2021 passed by the Adjudicating Officer/ADM cannot be sustained in law, and therefore, same is hereby set aside.
The sentence awarded by the Adjudicating Officer/ADM for contravention of Section 52 read with Section 49 of the FSS Act imposing penalty against the appellants are hereby set aside.
The FD of Rs.
3.50 Lacs placed on the record in compliance of direction of this Court dated 26.11.2021 be returned to the appellants.
20. The Record of the Adjudicating Officer /ADM be returned along with the copy of the order.
File of appeal be consigned to the Record Room.
